catalog_quote: Words in citation form are typically stressed on the final syllable, unless the final syllable nucleus is schwa. If the final syllable nucleus is schwa, then stress is on the last non-schwa vowel, which is typically in the penultimate syllable. The table below illustrates these stress generalizations for the word /tʃɑˈkɑt, dʒɑˈɡɑd/ ճակատ 'forehead' and several of its derived forms. In the forms with a full vowel in the final syllable, stress is word-final, no matter whether the word ends in an open syllable (row 2) or a closed syllable (rows 1, 3 and 5), or whether the word is unsuffixed (row 1), suffixed (rows 2–3) or a compound (row 5). The form /tʃɑˈkɑtət, dʒɑˈɡɑdətʰ/ ճակատդ (row 4) has a final schwa and penultimate stress. ... Clitics are unstressed ... new_statements.quote: Final stress systems are found in most dialects, and penultimate stress systems occur in Erevan, (Old) Julfa, Meghri, Agulis, Karabagh, Astraxan, and some subdialects of Mush. With the exception of Syria and Shamaxi, which have developed vowel length contrasts, Armenian dialects appear to be insensitive to prosodic weight distinctions. [...] Let us first consider the superficial facts of stress assignment in 'final stress' systems, represented here by the literary dialects. Primary stress is regularly assigned to the final full (i.e. non-epenthetic) vowel in a word, as in (27). [...] there are a number of words which contain no underlying vowels, and surface with one or more epenthetic schwas. Such words receive initial stress.

new_statements.relation_note: Same primary rule as the catalog (Seyfarth et al. 2024: final syllable unless its nucleus is schwa, then the last non-schwa vowel) and as Dolatian 2020 / Athanasopoulou et al. 2017: stress the final full vowel. Adds: initial secondary stress (with his own caveat), the ordinal/adverb/vocative/hypocoristic exceptions, and the penultimate-stress dialect type. One point of difference: for words whose only vowels are epenthetic schwas Vaux gives initial stress (SEA/SWA), while the catalog's Beirut speakers produce final stress (/fəsˈtəx/). Vaux also states outright that Armenian is insensitive to prosodic weight, which bears on the catalog's 'weight' kind label (the label encodes schwa-avoidance…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In the 'final stress' type (most dialects, including the literary Standard Eastern and Standard Western Armenian, and by Vaux's dialect list the western dialects such as Hamshen), primary stress falls on the last full (non-schwa, non-epenthetic) vowel of the word; a final epenthetic schwa is skipped, so stress lands on the preceding full vowel. Words with no full vowel at all (only epenthetic schwas) take initial stress. Syllable weight plays no role (Vaux says the dialects are insensitive to prosodic weight, except Syria and Shamaxi which have vowel length). A second type ('penultimate stress': Erevan, Julfa, Meghri, Agulis, Karabagh, Astraxan, some Mush) stresses the penultimate full vowel. The 'weight-sensitive' label here follows the catalog's convention of coding schwa-avoidance as weight; the sensitivity is to vowel quality (schwa vs full vowel), not to syllable weight.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 86: 'Finally, all Armenian dialects generally have secondary stress on the initial syllable, with some exceptions to be discussed in 2.3.3 and 2.3.4.' But p. 99 retracts confidence: 'the behavior of secondary stress in Armenian has not yet been established, and my informants are unable to provide satisfactory judgements regarding secondary stress.'
new_statements.exceptions: Ordinal numbers stress the final syllable of the root numeral, not the suffix (hing-erord > híngerord 'fifth'), unless that vowel is deleted (erku-erord > yerkrórd 'second') (pp. 83-84); a set of adverbs optionally take initial stress (híma ~ himá 'now', sireli ~ sirelí 'dear') (p. 84); vocatives of personal names optionally initial stress, obligatory in hypocoristics (Máro, Káro) (pp. 84-85); schwa-only words take initial stress, with the unexplained exception slpzt 'suddenly' [salapá zt] (p. 85, fn. 11); in some dialects (Erznka) vowelless words instead receive final stress (p. 103); Shatax negative verbs show lexical stress on the verb root's initial syllable (pp. 96-97); penultimate-stress dialects such as Karabagh stress the penultimate full vowel, with exceptional final-stress words, e.g. the plural -ner- always bears stress (pp. 86-87, 94-95, fn. 27).
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog's homs1234 is Homshetsma (Hamshen Armenian, spoken in northeast Turkey, Abkhazia and Krasnodar), but the catalog record filed under this code is Beirut Western Armenian, i.e. Standard Western Armenian as spoken in Beirut (Seyfarth et al. 2024). Of the two works: Vaux 2007 describes Homshetsma proper (northern and eastern subdialects) and is silent on stress; Vaux 1994 (the open stand-in for Vaux 1998) describes the literary dialects SEA and SWA plus named regional dialects (Karabagh, Agulis, Shatax, Erznka etc.), lists Hamshen among the western dialects in ch. 2 list (1) without discussing its stress, and never mentions Beirut. Its 'final stress' statement covers Standard Western Armenian and so applies to the catalog's variety; the code-to-name mismatch itself should be flagged to whoever maintains the catalog mapping.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on the primary rule: Vaux 1994 (final full vowel, schwa skipped), Seyfarth et al. 2024, Dolatian 2020 and Athanasopoulou et al. 2017 all give final stress that avoids a final schwa. Two minor points differ. (1) Schwa-only words: Vaux 1994 p. 85 says such words receive initial stress in the literary dialects (SEA/SWA), and notes dialects like Erznka where they receive final stress (p. 103); the catalog's Beirut speakers (Seyfarth et al. 2024) produce final stress (/fəsˈtəx/ 'pistachio'), so on this sub-case the catalog's source and Vaux differ. (2) Labeling: Vaux states 'Armenian dialects appear to be insensitive to prosodic weight distinctions' (p. 82-83), and Dolatian 2020 calls the system quantity-insensitive; the catalog's classification weight therefore has to be read as schwa-avoidance (vowel-quality sensitivity), not syllable-weight sensitivity. Vaux's claim of initial secondary stress (p. 86) is undercut by his own p. 99 admission that informants cannot judge secondary stress. Vaux 2007 is silent.

sources.quote: 'Armenian is similar to Turkish, with canonical stress on the final syllable (2a), and non-canonical stress preceding certain suffixes (2b). More generally, and differently from Turkish, however, the non-canonical stress is fully predictable since it just avoids any final syllable with a schwa, even if it does not involve a suffix (2c) [9=Vaux 1998].' Examples papak-í 'desire-GEN/DAT', papák-ə 'desire-DEF', yerpémən 'sometimes'. Instrumental (10 speakers): stressed vs unstressed vowels classified mainly by F0 in both final and penultimate positions.
sources.locator: p. 1398 sec. 2, ex. (2); stimuli p. 1399 sec. 4.2; results Table 3 p. 1400
sources.note: The instrumental study the JIPA domain quote relies on ('word-level stress is cued only by mean f0 and f0 excursion'); confirms final stress with schwa-avoidance on 10 Western Armenian speakers.

sources.note: Silent on stress. Also not about the catalog's variety: the chapter describes Homshetsma proper (northern and eastern subdialects of the Hamshen Armenians of northeast Turkey), which is what Glottolog's homs1234 denotes, whereas the catalog record under this code is Beirut Western Armenian (Seyfarth et al. 2024). Its content is orthography, dialect classification (Homshetsma vs Xodorchur, Trabzon, Artvin, Baberd, Erzerum), archaisms, innovations, lexical/phonological subdialect differences, and sample texts.
